Dialogue: I followed the address the shopkeeper had given me and spent a while searching the neighborhood before I finally spotted Annie.
She was standing by the roadside with a guitar in her arms. It looked like she’d just finished busking.
Hi. Are you Annie?
That’s me. Can I help you?
Did you know Elena?
The casual look on Annie’s face faltered for a moment.
Elena? …I haven’t heard that name in a long time.
I’m arranging her funeral. I’d like to get in touch with some people who knew her.
Her funeral?
She looked down and plucked a string.
So she’s dead.
Yes.
When did it happen?
Not long ago.
I see.
She looked down again, as though it had little to do with her.
Then what do you want with me? We haven’t spoken in years.
I just thought her old friends ought to know.
Friends?
She gave a little laugh.
Easy for you to say. It’s been years. Who remembers any of that now?
You remember her.
Annie didn’t answer.
If you want to know about back then, you can walk with me for a bit. I don’t have much to say, though.
All right.
Annie and I walked slowly down the street.
It was an old stretch of road, with worn storefronts on either side and walls covered in old ads and graffiti.
Annie took her time, stopping now and then to look at something by the roadside.
We used to hang around here all the time.
You and Elena?
Yeah. There wasn’t much to do back then, so we liked to wander around.
Did she come here often?
Of course. She used to live nearby, but she didn’t much like going home.
Why?
Well… I guess she didn’t much like the atmosphere at home.
She shrugged.
Her dad was an odd man. Elena found him exhausting to live with.
Is that why she went out so often?
Something like that.
She did not continue to explain.
I stopped outside an old repair shop.
There was a maintenance advertisement on the door, the paper was already yellow, and there were some references to old machine repairs and maintenance.
This store looks like it's been open for a long time.
Yeah, it was already here back then.
Did you two come here often?
Now and then. We used to wander around here, and whenever we passed this place, we’d stop and have a look.
Was Elena interested in this stuff too?
She’d look at everything. Even when she had no idea what something was, she’d go right up and spend ages trying to figure it out.
Sounds like fun.
It was fun.
She took a look at the ad.
Looking back, everything seemed fun back then.
And now?
Now? They just look like old ads to me.
She kept walking.
Old graffiti covered parts of the wall. Newer ads had been pasted over some of it, leaving only faint patches of color.
There's a lot of graffiti here.
There used to be even more.
You guys used to play here?
Once, Elena scribbled all over the wall with chalk and got told off by someone passing by.
Elena did stuff like that?
Why not? She wouldn't dare to do that at home.
Because of her father?
Yeah. Her dad didn’t like her wasting time on things like that.
She paused.
I think she just wanted to do something she liked. It wasn’t a big deal.
Did she complain to you about things at home?
Sometimes. But she didn’t always complain. Sometimes she’d start making excuses for her dad halfway through.
Why?
Because she felt she shouldn’t blame him.
Annie looked down and kicked a pebble aside.
That’s how she was. She was unhappy herself, but she always wondered if she’d done something wrong.
I walked over to the bus stop sign.
A few old ads were stuck to the sign, and the route information was hard to make out.
Did you two take this bus often?
All the time. Sometimes after school we’d take the bus somewhere else.
Where to?
Nowhere in particular. We went wherever we felt like going.
Did Elena like going out?
Of course. She always thought the outside world was more interesting than home.
Did she say where she wanted to go?
She named all sorts of places, but most of the time she was just talking.
She smiled.
One time she said she had to get out of here, somewhere where nobody knew her.
Did she say that?
Well, I asked her, what should I do?
What did she say?
She said let's go together.
Annie stopped for a second.
But in the end, we didn't make it.
Why didn't you keep contacting her?
She had her life and I had mine. And then...
She didn't finish.
There's a big tree in the middle of the street, and there's an old bench under it.
We used to sit here a lot.
This tree looks very old.
Yeah. It was so big by then.
What do you normally talk about sitting here?
Talk about everything.
She thought about it.
Talk about school, talk about it, talk about things that can't be done.
Like what?
You know, where you're going, what you're going to do, what you're going to do, what you're going to do, what you're going to do, go out every day.
Sounds free.
It was true at the time that everything would have been better if we had just left.
Is that what Elena thinks?
She wants to leave more than I do.
And did she realize it later?
Annie didn't answer.
After a while, she whispered.
No, I don't.
There was an old man sitting under the tree with an old guitar on his knee.
He's defibrating the chords and occasionally plays a few simple notes.
The old man's still here.
You know him?
Of course. He played here before.
The old man heard us, looked up and looked at us.
Yo, it's you, little girl. It's been a long time.
I've been busy.
Or the guitar?
Yeah.
How's it going?
Same as always.
The old man laughed.
I can't do that. I can't play the piano. I can't do it.
Got it, got it.
Did you meet here often?
Yeah. Sometimes we'll sit here and listen to him play.
You two little girls used to sit next to each other for half a day.
And Elena?
The old man stunned.
Elena the little girl.
Yeah.
She used to like to listen to me play. Every time I came through here, I had to stop and listen.
Does she play guitar?
A little, but it's not good.
She just likes to try everything.
The kid's interesting.
The old man's head was down and he touched the chord.
Too bad I haven't seen her in a while.
She's dead.
The old man stopped moving.
I see.
He's been quiet for a while.
That's a shame.
Annie didn't talk.
I looked at her, and I looked at the old man.
Maybe Elena used to know more people than I thought.
Let's keep moving.
Speaking of which, why the hell would you give her a funeral?
Because I think she should have a funeral.
People are dead. What's the point of doing this?
At least let the people who remember her see her last face.
You're a strange person.
Don't you want to come?
I didn't say no.
She looked down at her guitar.
Actually, we met at the school music class.
You were in the same class?
Well, there was a music teacher at the school, and we liked her.
Is that why you're familiar?
Something like that. She used to practice with me, though she didn't have a reputation.
You guys used to be close?
Sure.
She smiled a little.
She kind of liked to tell me strange ideas about where to live and what to do later.
Sounds like she's been trying to get out of here.
Yeah. She always thought that if she left the house, she could start a new life.
Do you think she's happy?
Annie was silent for a long time.
I don't know.
But she was really happy at least for a while.
Would you like to come to her funeral?
She took a look at me.
You've come all the way here. Can I say no?
Thank you.
Don't thank me. I just feel that something has to come to an end.
She's holding back the guitar in her arms.
And I have something to say to her.
Okay.
By the way, if you want to know her later, you can go to the old music teacher. She should remember a lot of things.
What's the teacher's name?
Maria.
Okay, I'll find her.
Let's do this.
I watched her leave the street and slowly went to the other side.
I think, at least this time, Elena's gonna have another person at the funeral who knows her.
